metadata.title: A graphically based machine learning approach to predict secondary schools performance in Tunisia

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 school and student data aggregated to the secondary-school level (105 public secondary schools after exclusions). The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme when estimating the first-stage DDF/DEA inefficiency scores or when training the second-stage regression tree and random forest models. Because the analysis is conducted on school-level aggregates derived from a complex survey design, standard practice would be to use PISA student/school weights (and replicate weights if available) to obtain population-representative uncertainty; however, the paper provides no weight variable names or survey-design adjustments. For replication, analysts should check the PISA 2012 Data/School files for appropriate weight variables and decide whether to incorporate them via survey-weighted estimation or design-aware resampling; if weights are omitted, results should be interpreted as descriptive/predictive rather than strictly generalizable.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Data are extracted from PISA 2012 (school and student dataset). The analysis is restricted to public secondary schools by eliminating 153 secondary schools that are private. All observations with missing data are removed, resulting in a final sample of 105 secondary schools for the school year 2011–2012. The first-stage DDF/DEA uses school-level inputs (weekly learning time in mathematics, science, and language) and outputs (school averages of PISA mathematics, reading, and science scores) plus a bad output (principal-reported dropout proportion). The second-stage ML models predict the first-stage estimated inefficiency score using six school-level covariates (class size, school size, school location, proportion of girls, competition, parental pressure).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 (school and student data), Tunisia; secondary schools (school year 2011–2012); school-level efficiency via DDF/DEA
main_findings.target_variable: School inefficiency score (DDF/DEA distance to frontier)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Regression tree: reported node means and split structure; no global accuracy metric reported. Random forest: 1000 trees; variable importance ranges reported (e.g., school size 46.517%, proportion of girls 47.773%, class size 21.022%, competition 10.499%, location 10.913%, parental pressure 8.492%). OLS and Tobit robustness models reported significance at 5% for competition and school location (OLS: COMP p=0.020, SCHLOC p=0.037; Tobit: COMP p=0.019, SCHLOC p=0.042).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 data aggregated to Tunisian public secondary schools, the study leveraged school size, proportion of girls, class size, competition, and school location to predict school inefficiency (distance-to-frontier) from a DDF/DEA first stage, finding that school size and girls’ proportion were the most influential predictors in the random-forest importance ranking while competition and rural location were associated with higher inefficiency in linear robustness checks. This indicates that improving secondary-school performance in Tunisia may require targeted organizational policies (e.g., managing school/class size and gender composition) alongside reducing counterproductive competitive pressures and addressing disadvantages linked to rural settings, though the paper’s predictive ML results are not presented with survey-weighted uncertainty and causality cannot be inferred.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2012 school and student data for Tunisia, restricting the analytic sample to 105 public secondary schools after excluding private schools and removing observations with missing data. In a first stage, it computes school-level inefficiency using a directional distance function (DEA) that combines three desirable outputs (school-average PISA mathematics, reading, and science scores summarized across plausible values) and one undesirable output (principal-reported dropout proportion), with three inputs (weekly learning time in mathematics, science, and language). In the second stage, it trains regression trees and random forests in R to predict the continuous inefficiency score and to visualize nonlinear interactions; random forests use 1000 trees and report variable importance shares (notably school size and proportion of girls). Robustness is assessed with OLS and Tobit models, where competition and school location are significant at the 5% level. Limitations include lack of reported survey-weight usage and the fact that ML feature importance and tree splits are predictive associations rather than causal effects.
